analysis.one_liner: Raises taxes on snuff and chewing tobacco to cigarette levels to fund anti-tobacco education.
analysis.headline: The bill would have raised the federal snuff tax from 36 cents to $4.25 a pound, but it never received a vote in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal excise tax on snuff from 36 cents to $4.25 a pound and on chewing tobacco from 12 cents to $1.12 a pound, bringing those taxes in line with the tax on small cigarettes. Ten percent of the new revenue would have gone into a new Smokeless Tobacco Education and Prevention Trust Fund to pay for public education about the health risks of smokeless tobacco and programs to reduce its use. The bill was referred to two House committees in September 1993 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Young people who might otherwise start using smokeless tobacco, since higher prices are the most proven deterrent to starting. Current users who would quit or cut back, and the families spared the mouth and throat cancers that smokeless tobacco causes. The public also gains from a funded education campaign about the risks, and the general Treasury gains the other 90 percent of new revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Young people and smokeless tobacco users

how_it_helps.text: Raised the federal excise tax on snuff from 36 cents to $4.25 a pound and on chewing tobacco from 12 cents to $1.12 a pound, roughly matching the tax level on small cigarettes, and tied future smokeless tobacco tax rates to any future cigarette tax increases.
Higher tobacco prices are the most reliable tool for cutting use, especially among young people; the bill's stated purpose was to reduce smokeless tobacco consumption and fund programs to do so.

Created a Smokeless Tobacco Education and Prevention Trust Fund, reserving 10 percent of the net new revenue for public education about the risks of smokeless tobacco, which causes mouth and throat cancers.

analysis.who_pays: Smokeless tobacco users, who would pay sharply higher prices starting the day of enactment, and manufacturers and wholesalers, who would face the new tax plus an additional tax on inventory already in their warehouses when the bill took effect. Retail sales through the supply chain would shrink as use declined.
analysis.who_pays_short: Smokeless tobacco makers and their customers

drawbacks.text: The tax would have fallen directly on users, who skew toward lower-income, rural, and working-class men, raising their cost of an existing habit immediately on enactment.

Only 10 percent of the new revenue was dedicated to education and prevention; the other 90 percent would have gone to the general Treasury, making this partly a revenue bill rather than a pure public-health measure.

The tax took effect on the day of enactment, with an extra $3.87-per-pound tax on snuff already held for sale in non-retail inventories, a cost that wholesalers and distributors would pass through to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health logic is sound: tobacco taxes reduce use, and smokeless tobacco was taxed at a small fraction of the cigarette rate despite causing oral cancers. The honest tradeoffs are that the tax is regressive for existing users, most of the money would not have gone to prevention, and the immediate effective date with an inventory tax hit wholesalers hard. A better-designed version might phase the tax in and dedicate a larger share to education, but the core trade — higher prices for a cancer-causing product in exchange for funded prevention — favored the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees in September 1993, sent to a health subcommittee a month later, and never got a markup, a floor vote, or a Senate companion before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Patricia Schroeder introduced the bill on September 8, 1993, joined by four original cosponsors, and it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees.
Fourteen Democratic cosponsors signed on in total, all from one party; no Republican ever supported the bill.

On October 5, 1993, the Energy and Commerce Committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, and neither that subcommittee nor the Ways and Means Committee, which handles tax bills, ever took further action.
The bill sat with no committee vote and no floor action until the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, at which point it died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Smokeless tobacco manufacturers and distributors are better off because the bill died: they kept the 36-cent and 12-cent tax rates instead of a twelvefold increase on snuff, with no tax on existing inventories. Users kept cheaper product, but no education program about the risks was ever funded.

for.name: Patricia Schroeder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on September 8, 1993.

for.name: 14 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; original cosponsors Dick Durbin, Michael Andrews, Mike Synar, and Eleanor Holmes Norton joined the introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (chaired by Dan Rostenkowski)
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup or reported the bill.

against.name: Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 5, 1993, and took no further action on it.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed tobacco tax increases and consumption-reduction measures during this era.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so no one ever had to record a position.

industries.note: The snuff tax would have jumped from 36 cents to $4.25 a pound — roughly a twelvefold increase — with an additional tax on warehouse inventories, and the bill's explicit goal was to shrink the market for their product. Keeping the tax at 36 cents kept the product cheap and sales intact.
They would have owed a new tax on existing non-retail inventory and faced shrinking sales as higher prices cut use. Retailers were spared the inventory tax on stock already on their shelves.
